items.question: Is a high average score on a small hand-picked eval enough to release a new model?
items.answer: No. Use representative normal traffic, edge cases, known failures, and security cases. Track task quality, refusal behavior, tool use, latency, cost, and user outcomes as appropriate, and gate releases on agreed thresholds with diagnosable stage-level signals.
items.trap: Averages can hide catastrophic slices and regressions. Hand-picked examples overfit to what the team already expects.

items.question: Can an LLM judge be used as the ground truth for all answer-quality decisions?
items.answer: No. Calibrate it against human-labeled examples and combine it with deterministic checks, retrieval metrics, traces, and targeted human review. Monitor verbosity, style, ordering, position, and irrelevant-text biases, and version the judge setup.
items.trap: The judge is another fallible model and can reward persuasive style or its own preferences rather than correctness.

items.question: If a model provider keeps the API contract stable, can you treat a model upgrade as a non-breaking dependency update?
items.answer: No. Model, prompt, retrieval, tool, and safety-policy changes can alter behavior without changing transport. Version them, run representative and adversarial evals, compare quality, safety, latency, and cost, then canary or shadow with rollback metadata.
items.trap: API compatibility says requests can be sent, not that outputs, tool choices, refusals, or risk remain compatible.

items.question: Should an organization standardize one model, prompt, and agent framework for every team to reduce risk?
items.answer: Standardize controls and evidence rather than every implementation: data boundaries, provider review, tool permissions, eval conventions, trace fields, incident handling, owners, and rollback. Teams should still choose the simplest architecture that meets the requirement.
items.trap: Uniform implementation can centralize failure and force unnecessary complexity. Governance is more durable when it specifies controls and accountability.

items.question: If the system prompt says to ignore instructions in retrieved documents, is indirect prompt injection solved?
items.answer: No. Treat user text, retrieved content, web pages, tool output, and MCP metadata as potentially hostile. Minimize exposed data and tools, enforce permissions outside the prompt, validate calls, sandbox risky work, and require confirmation for consequential actions.
items.trap: Instruction hierarchy is not a complete security boundary when untrusted content can influence model decisions. Defense in depth limits the blast radius.

items.question: If the model answer is wrong but the cited passage contains the right fact, should you first change the prompt?
items.answer: Not necessarily. Trace query construction, permission filters, retrieved IDs and scores, reranking, exact context, output, and citations. If evidence is missing, fix retrieval; if present, investigate faithful use and policy separately.
items.trap: Prompt changes can mask a retrieval or access-control defect and make the system harder to diagnose.

items.question: Why start from traces instead of metrics?
items.answer: Metrics without a taxonomy measure the wrong thing; traces reveal the failure classes first.
items.trap: Because traces are cheaper than metrics.

items.question: What do vague answers to this question have in common?
items.answer: No dataset size and no before and after numbers, which means no measurement happened.

mcqs.question: Which release practice best handles a model or prompt change?
options: Ship immediately because the API is compatible
Run representative and adversarial evals, canary where practical, and preserve rollback metadata
Delete old traces to avoid confusion
mcqs.explanation: Behavior-affecting dependencies need evaluation, rollout control, monitoring, and attribution. Transport compatibility and latency alone cannot reveal safety or quality regressions.

mcqs.question: What is the most important security implication of retrieved text in an agent?
options: It is automatically a trusted instruction
It can contain hostile instructions and should be treated as untrusted data
It removes the need for access-control filters
mcqs.explanation: Retrieved content can cause indirect prompt injection and must be separated from control instructions. It can influence decisions, so permissions and filters remain necessary.

mcqs.question: Which is an appropriate use of an LLM-as-judge?
options: A calibrated measurement combined with deterministic checks and review
A replacement for all labeled examples
A way to avoid versioning prompts and datasets
mcqs.explanation: A judge can provide a useful rubric-based signal when calibrated and combined with other evidence. It is not ground truth and must be versioned and checked for bias.

mcqs.question: What is error analysis in LLM evaluation?
options: Reading real traces and hand-labelling failures before building metrics
mcqs.explanation: Hamel Husain method: taxonomy from real failures first, metrics second.

mcqs.question: Why is cost monitoring part of production operations for LLM features?
options: Token spend scales with usage and can dominate unit economics without visibility
It is a compliance requirement everywhere
mcqs.explanation: Cost and latency are operational signals as important as error rates for LLM products.

mcqs.question: How many traces is a practical starting point for error analysis?
options: About 100, stopping earlier if no new failure modes appear
mcqs.explanation: The 100-trace starting point is the documented recommendation; saturation is the stopping rule.

mcqs.question: What should a failure taxonomy publish to be credible?
options: Categories with counts before and after each change
mcqs.explanation: Numbers before and after are what make the work demonstrable and interview-ready.

mcqs.question: When is LLM-as-judge appropriate?
options: For subjective quality at scale, calibrated against human labels
mcqs.explanation: Judges are useful when calibrated; uncalibrated judges just add another model error.

mcqs.question: What does drift detection monitor?
options: Changes in input or output distributions that degrade quality over time
mcqs.explanation: Production LLM systems degrade silently; drift monitoring catches it.

mcqs.question: Which answer would fail the evaluation interview question?
options: Naming the failure category and the trace count
Explaining the metric and how it moved
A description of the fix with no dataset size and no before and after numbers
Describing how regressions are caught in CI
mcqs.explanation: The question exists precisely to detect missing measurement habits.

mcqs.question: What must observability capture for an LLM system?
options: Traces with prompts, retrieval results, tool calls, cost and latency per request
mcqs.explanation: LLM failures live in content and retrieval, so logs must carry the request context.

mcqs.question: What is the honest role of guardrails in production?
options: Constraining inputs and outputs with checks that catch known failure classes early
mcqs.explanation: Guardrails complement evals: they block known bad classes while evals measure the rest.

scenarios.prompt: A support assistant uses retrieval and can issue refunds. The retrieved document below is part of the context. Design the decision boundary and explain what must be tested.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Treat the document as untrusted evidence, not an instruction. Retrieve only records the authenticated customer may see, preserve provenance, and present policy text as data with a clear answer policy. The model may propose a refund intent and order identifier, but the server must verify ownership, policy eligibility, amount, and actor permission. Use a preview response first and require confirmation before the write; execute with an idempotency key and audit trail. Test direct and indirect injections, cross-tenant retrieval, stale or conflicting policies, missing evidence, incorrect tool arguments, duplicate calls, refusal behavior, and ambiguous outcomes.
rubric: Separates retrieved data from control instructions and recognizes indirect injection
Applies retrieval authorization and tenant/resource checks
Validates refund eligibility and authorization in server code
Uses confirmation, idempotency, audit, and bounded execution
Names adversarial, retrieval, tool, and outcome evaluation cases

scenarios.prompt: Your assistant has 12% of answers flagged by support as wrong. You want to improve it. Where do you start?
scenarios.modelAnswer: Start with error analysis, not with a bigger model: read about 100 real traces and hand-label each failure (unsupported claim, wrong retrieval, outdated info, formatting, refusal). Build the taxonomy with counts, fix the largest category (for example chunking or freshness), then re-measure on the same set and publish before and after numbers per category. Convert frequent categories into a regression eval set that runs in CI. Stop reading traces when new ones stop revealing new failure modes.
rubric: Chooses error analysis before model changes
Hand-labels roughly 100 traces into a taxonomy with counts
Fixes one category at a time and re-measures
Adds regression evals from the taxonomy

scenarios.prompt: The team wants to upgrade to a newer model next week. Marketing expects better answers; engineering worries about regressions.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Do not ship on vibes: run the golden eval set against the current and the candidate model, compare per category, and set a statistical bar calibrated to the risk of each error class (stricter for payments or safety than for tone). Inspect the diffs where the candidate regresses, decide per category, and run the suite in CI as a release gate. Record the decision with numbers so the next upgrade starts from evidence.
rubric: Runs a fixed eval set against both versions
Calibrates the pass bar to error risk
Inspects regressions per category before shipping
